# Dissipative phases, steady states, and metastability {#sec-dissipative-phases}

Equilibrium phase transitions organize states that minimize a free energy. An open driven system instead balances coherent motion, pumping, and loss. It can sustain currents, choose an ordered state, or oscillate without possessing a Gibbs distribution. Dissipation is not merely a perturbation to a phase diagram: it can create the phase itself.

We begin with a finite-dimensional Markovian equation $\dot\rho=\mathcal L\rho$, where $\mathcal L\rho=-i[H,\rho]+\sum_\mu\mathcal D[L_\mu]\rho$. The essential questions are whether a stationary state exists, whether it is unique, how it is approached, and which properties become singular when system size grows. These questions must be separated. A state annihilated by all jumps need not be the unique steady state, and a long-lived finite-system plateau need not be a thermodynamic phase.

## Stationarity, darkness, and uniqueness

A stationary state satisfies $\mathcal L\rho_{\mathrm{ss}}=0$. In finite dimension at least one exists. For example, time-average the channel evolution of an initial state over $[0,T]$. Compactness gives accumulation points, and the change under any fixed additional time interval vanishes as $T$ grows, producing an invariant state.

A **dark state** $|D\rangle$ is annihilated by every jump, $L_\mu|D\rangle=0$. If it is also an eigenstate of $H$, its projector is stationary. This is a sufficient condition. More generally, pure steady states can be simultaneous eigenstates of shifted jump operators, with a corresponding Hamiltonian consistency condition; the zero-eigenvalue dark-state criterion is convenient but not the most general theorem.

The vacuum of a lossy hopping model is dark. Every number state is unaffected by pure number dephasing at the instant its density matrix is diagonal, although the Hamiltonian can subsequently move it. A jump that annihilates an interesting target proves only that the target is stationary. Other invariant subspaces may prevent generic initial states from reaching it.

Uniqueness can often be checked by the operator algebra generated by $H$, jumps, and their adjoints, together with irreducibility assumptions. In practice, inspect symmetries and dark subspaces first, then compute the nullspace for small systems. An apparent single zero eigenvalue at one size is useful evidence but does not prove uniform mixing as size increases.

## Derivation: dissipative preparation of a Bell pair

The Bell state $|\Phi^+\rangle=(|00\rangle+|11\rangle)/\sqrt2$ has stabilizers $S_1=Z_1Z_2$ and $S_2=X_1X_2$. They commute and have a one-dimensional joint $+1$ eigenspace. Let $P_a^-=(I-S_a)/2$ project onto a violated stabilizer. Choose correction operators $C_1=X_1$ and $C_2=Z_2$. Each anticommutes with its own stabilizer and commutes with the other. Define

$$
L_1=\sqrt\kappa X_1P_1^-,\qquad L_2=\sqrt\kappa Z_2P_2^-.
$$ {#eq-diss-bell-jumps}

First, both jumps annihilate $|\Phi^+\rangle$. Second, a jump in channel $a$ maps a state with $S_a=-1$ into the $S_a=+1$ sector without changing the other syndrome. Third, the adjoint dissipator acting on $P_a^-$ is $-\kappa P_a^-$ for its own channel and zero for the other. Therefore

$$
\frac{d}{dt}\langle P_1^-+P_2^-\rangle=-\kappa\langle P_1^-+P_2^-\rangle.
$$ {#eq-diss-syndrome-decay}

At stationarity both nonnegative violation probabilities vanish. A positive density matrix with no weight in either violated sector is supported on the one-dimensional common kernel. Hence the Bell projector is the unique stationary state for $H=0$. This argument establishes convergence of syndrome probabilities and uniqueness rather than merely checking darkness.

The construction generalizes to stabilizer-state pumping, but locality and compatibility matter. A correction for one many-body stabilizer can disturb others, and a local implementation may require ancillas or several steps. Theoretical dissipative preparation schemes demonstrate possibility; their mixing times and physical resources determine usefulness [@info-verstraete2009].

## Derivation: relaxation modes and metastable plateaus

Suppose for now that $\mathcal L$ is diagonalizable. Its right and left eigenmatrices obey

$$
\mathcal L R_a=\lambda_aR_a,\quad
\mathcal L^\dagger L_a=\lambda_a^*L_a,\quad
\operatorname{Tr}(L_a^\dagger R_b)=\delta_{ab}.
$$ {#eq-diss-biorthogonal}

For a unique stationary state choose $R_0=\rho_{\mathrm{ss}},L_0=I$. Expanding the initial state gives

$$
\rho(t)=\rho_{\mathrm{ss}}+\sum_{a\ne0}c_ae^{\lambda_at}R_a,
\qquad c_a=\operatorname{Tr}(L_a^\dagger\rho_0).
$$ {#eq-diss-mode-expansion}

An observable sees coefficients $c_a\operatorname{Tr}(OR_a)$, so its slowest visible decay can differ from the smallest nonzero $-\operatorname{Re}\lambda_a$. A mode with zero overlap is absent from that observable or initial condition.

If one real decay rate $\epsilon$ is much smaller than the rest, there is an interval $\Delta_{\mathrm{fast}}^{-1}\ll t\ll\epsilon^{-1}$ in which fast modes have decayed but the slow mode has not. States appear trapped near a low-dimensional **metastable manifold**. At later times they still approach the unique stationary state.

A classical two-state model captures the mechanism. Let rates $k_{12}$ and $k_{21}$ connect two long-lived configurations. For the probability $p_1$,

$$
\dot p_1=-k_{12}p_1+k_{21}(1-p_1),\quad
p_1^{\mathrm{ss}}=\frac{k_{21}}{k_{12}+k_{21}},\quad
\Delta=k_{12}+k_{21}.
$$ {#eq-diss-two-state}

Small rates yield long switching times and history dependence over finite observation windows. They do not create two exact stationary states at finite size. If both rates vanish exponentially with system size while their ratio changes sharply with a control parameter, a thermodynamic first-order transition can emerge. This elementary model explains why hysteresis and bimodal observations require time-scale and size analysis.

## Nonnormality and exceptional points

A Liouvillian need not commute with its adjoint. Such a matrix is **nonnormal**, so its eigenvectors can be nearly linearly dependent. The spectral gap alone then gives an incomplete account of finite-time relaxation: large expansion coefficients or poorly conditioned eigenvectors can produce a long transient before asymptotic decay is visible.

At an **exceptional point**, eigenvalues and eigenvectors coalesce. A Jordan block with eigenvalue $\lambda$ contributes $e^{\lambda t}(I+tN+\cdots)$, where $N$ is nilpotent. Polynomial factors modify relaxation even though the real parts of the eigenvalues remain nonpositive. Physical channel evolution remains contractive in appropriate state-distance measures; large transients in arbitrary operator coordinates do not permit amplification of distinguishability between physical states under the same channel.

Numerically, compare direct time evolution, singular values of the propagator in a stated norm, and spectral predictions. Small residuals for individual eigenvectors do not guarantee an accurately reconstructed propagator near an ill-conditioned degeneracy. Report conditioning and use a Schur decomposition when an eigenvector expansion is unstable.

## What constitutes a dissipative phase transition?

For finite dimension and generic parameters, stationary observables are smooth except at exact degeneracies or other singular constructions. A many-body transition normally concerns a nonanalytic thermodynamic limit. The order of limits matters:

$$
\lim_{L\to\infty}\lim_{t\to\infty}\rho_L(t)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\lim_{t\to\infty}\lim_{L\to\infty}\rho_L(t)
$$ {#eq-diss-limits}

can describe different state selections. A finite system with a symmetry often has a unique symmetric steady state, while an infinite system admits symmetry-broken stationary states selected by weak fields or initial conditions.

For a continuous transition, a correlation length diverges and a relaxation gap often closes as $\Delta\sim\xi^{-z}$, defining a dynamic exponent $z$. At criticality finite-size scaling may give $\Delta_L\sim L^{-z}$. These relations need an identified universality class and suitable observables. A small gap caused by a conserved hydrodynamic mode throughout a phase is not by itself a transition diagnostic.

Minganti and collaborators connect steady-state structure and low Liouvillian modes for dissipative transitions [@info-minganti2018]. The practical lesson is to analyze eigenmatrices and observables together, not only a curve of the gap. A first-order switching mode, a critical order-parameter mode, and a diffusive conservation mode can all become slow for different reasons.

## Worked model: a driven lossy bosonic mode

Consider

$$
H=-\Delta a^\dagger a+\frac U2a^{\dagger2}a^2+F(a+a^\dagger),\qquad
L=\sqrt\kappa a.
$$ {#eq-diss-kerr}

The exact equation for $\alpha=\langle a\rangle$ is

$$
\dot\alpha=(i\Delta-\kappa/2)\alpha-iU\langle a^\dagger aa\rangle-iF.
$$

Factorizing $\langle a^\dagger aa\rangle\simeq|\alpha|^2\alpha$ gives a mean-field equation. Setting its derivative to zero and taking the modulus yields

$$
n[(\Delta-Un)^2+(\kappa/2)^2]=F^2,\qquad n=|\alpha|^2.
$$ {#eq-diss-kerr-cubic}

The cubic can have three positive solutions; their dynamical stability follows by linearizing the coupled equations for $\delta\alpha$ and $\delta\alpha^*$. Merely counting roots does not establish which are stable.

For one finite mode with a sufficiently converged Fock cutoff, quantum fluctuations generally connect mean-field attractors. A unique stationary state and switching can replace literal bistability. A sharp dissipative transition requires an appropriate limit, for example a scaling of nonlinearity and drive that sends occupation large, or an extended array. State that limit before describing the cubic as a phase diagram. Check cutoff convergence in the occupation distribution, not only the mean.

## Baths that generate many-body order

For lattice bosons, an illustrative number-conserving bond jump is

$$
L_{ij}=\sqrt\kappa\,(b_i^\dagger+b_j^\dagger)(b_i-b_j).
$$ {#eq-diss-condensate-jump}

The annihilation factor removes antisymmetric occupation, while the creation factor restores particles in the symmetric mode. On a connected graph, a uniform condensate at fixed particle number is dark because $(b_i-b_j)|D_N\rangle=0$. This gives a physical route to building coherence through dissipation. Interactions compete with the preferred dark-state structure and produce mixed stationary correlations.

Diehl and collaborators developed reservoir-engineered quantum matter in this spirit [@info-diehl2008]. Their work motivates a distinct research question from cooling to a Hamiltonian ground state: which correlations are selected by the jump structure itself? Establishing darkness is the first step; proving uniqueness, estimating the gap, and assessing the actual reservoir implementation are separate steps. In low dimensions, phase fluctuations can also invalidate a naïve mean-field ordered state.

Open-system symmetries come in several forms. A unitary $U$ can leave the complete generator covariant, $\mathcal L(U\rho U^\dagger)=U\mathcal L(\rho)U^\dagger$, without every jump individually commuting with $U$. Stronger commutation conditions can produce invariant sectors and multiple stationary states. Distinguish covariance of the evolution from conservation of a physical charge before applying equilibrium symmetry-breaking language.

## Boundary-driven transport

Reservoirs at the ends of a chain can sustain a stationary current. In the bulk, the adjoint generator gives a continuity equation $\dot n_j=j_{j-1}-j_j$ if no bulk source is present. Thus the steady current is spatially constant. Boundary driving breaks equilibrium but offers an operational transport experiment.

For a diffusive system in a suitable weak-bias regime,

$$
j\simeq-D\frac{n_R-n_L}{L}.
$$ {#eq-diss-fick}

A ballistic system can instead have a current remaining finite as length grows. Boundary resistance, contact-induced profiles, and nonlinear response can obscure this distinction in short chains. Vary length, bias, and reservoir coupling independently. A flat density profile by itself does not prove ballistic bulk transport.

Quadratic open fermion models provide exact benchmarks through third quantization [@info-prosen2008]. Interacting boundary-driven chains then connect dissipative numerics to bulk hydrodynamics. For those comparisons, distinguish a boundary Lindblad model used as a controlled drive from a microscopic derivation of a particular thermal contact.

## Research bridge: accelerated relaxation and state selection

The mode expansion also explains anomalous relaxation. A state farther from stationarity according to a chosen distance can relax faster if it has smaller overlap with the slowest mode. This is one mechanism behind quantum Mpemba phenomena. The conclusion depends on the distance, initial-state family, and whether dynamics is open or isolated; several effects share the name without sharing one mechanism.

A reproducible first project studies the Kerr mode or a short driven spin chain. Compute several low modes and left eigenmatrices, prepare initial states with different slow-mode overlaps, and compare their trace distance or a stated observable deviation. Check early-time crossings separately from asymptotic rates. Then increase Hilbert-space cutoff or chain length. The open question is which observed acceleration survives the physically relevant scaling limit and imperfections, rather than being a convenient finite-dimensional overlap cancellation.

The broader frontier concerns dissipative criticality with conservation laws, genuinely mixed-state orders, and feedback-stabilized quantum matter. Each proposal should identify the state or channel observable that distinguishes phases and a preparation or measurement protocol that can access it. A label borrowed from equilibrium is useful only after its operational meaning is specified.

## Two-time correlations probe more than a stationary density

Two generators can have the same stationary state and different dynamics. A maximally mixed steady state, for example, does not determine a relaxation rate or transport coefficient. In a Markovian setting with the assumptions underlying the quantum regression relation, a stationary two-time correlator can be written as $\langle A(t)B(0)\rangle_{\mathrm{ss}}=\operatorname{Tr}[A e^{t\mathcal L}(B\rho_{\mathrm{ss}})]$. The initial operator $B\rho_{\mathrm{ss}}$ need not itself be a physical density matrix, but the linear propagator acts on it unambiguously.

Expanding this expression in Liouvillian modes shows which frequencies and decay rates a given probe can see. A soft mode may be almost invisible in a chosen local correlator because its matrix element is small. Conversely, a conserved density can produce a slow correlator without any ordering transition. Spectroscopy and stationary snapshots therefore answer complementary questions.

For an experiment, select the probe by the proposed order parameter or conserved field, derive its expected finite-size scaling, and compare multiple observation times. A long-lived oscillatory response in a finite driven system can be a damped mode; an asymptotic oscillatory phase requires a carefully stated many-body or large-occupation limit. Treating every narrow spectral peak as a phase of time-dependent order would confuse lifetime with symmetry breaking.

## Exercises

1. **Bell pumping.** Verify every commutation relation used in @eq-diss-bell-jumps. Derive the syndrome decay and prove uniqueness using positivity of the stationary density matrix.
2. **Metastability.** Solve @eq-diss-two-state for arbitrary $p_1(0)$. Suppose both rates scale as $e^{-aL}$; identify which observation times distinguish a metastable plateau from stationarity.
3. **Exceptional point.** Exponentiate the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}-\gamma&1\\0&-\gamma\end{pmatrix}$. Explain why fitting its coordinates to a single exponential can give a time-dependent apparent rate.
4. **Kerr physics.** Derive the cubic and linear stability matrix. Compare its roots with a truncated quantum steady-state calculation at increasing cutoffs. Identify what further limit would justify a phase-transition claim.
5. **Transport protocol.** Design a boundary-driven study distinguishing $j\propto L^{-1}$ from a contact-limited crossover. Include bias dependence, density profiles, and uncertainty.

::: {.callout-tip title="Worked solutions: exercises 2 and 3"}
The two-state solution is $p_1(t)=p_1^{\mathrm{ss}}+[p_1(0)-p_1^{\mathrm{ss}}]e^{-(k_{12}+k_{21})t}$. If both rates vanish as $e^{-aL}$, any polynomial observation time can appear stationary within one metastable configuration, while the true stationary mixture requires times of order $e^{aL}$.

Write the Jordan matrix as $-\gamma I+N$, with $N^2=0$. Its exponential is $e^{-\gamma t}(I+tN)$. A coordinate proportional to $te^{-\gamma t}$ has logarithmic decay rate $\gamma-1/t$, so a single-exponential fit can drift even in an exactly known linear problem.
:::
